newsitem.title: USA: Merrill Lynch strategist bullish on Japan.
newsitem.headline: Merrill Lynch strategist bullish on Japan.

text.p: Japan's resilient economy is capable of outperforming current market expectations, especially with the help of a weaker yen, a strategist for Merrill Lynch and Co Inc said Thursday.
Chief investment strategist Charles Clough said Japan's government and business leaders were starting to carry out reforms needed to open up the economy.

"We think the economy will surprise on the upside, and its resiliency so far ... is improving confidence both in the business and consumer sector there," he said in a conference call accompanied by Merrill Lynch analysts.
He listed four areas for optimism:

-- Indications of a strengthening economy, including lower inventories, rising industrial production estimates and steady retail sales. "The underlying economy has been stronger than expected and the (recent) consumption tax hike seems to have been shrugged off."

-- Improvement in banks' problem debts and government approval for broader ties between Japanese and foreign financial institutions. For example, Bankers Trust has begun a tie-up with troubled Nippon Credit Bank Ltd.

-- Government and business have begun restructuring efforts. The government has promised no more tax hikes, and businesses are starting stock options and other measures to reward performance. With the advantages of a weaker yen and ongoing efforts to cut costs, "Japanese earnings continue to surprise us on the upside," Clough said.
-- Japanese stocks are especially attractive when they are valued against cash flow rather than reported earnings per share.
"We've thought for some time that the sky-high multiples in Japan were a little bit contrived," he said.

For example, Nippon Telegraph and Telephone has a price/earnings ratio of 49 on estimated 1998 earnings, but a multiple of 5.6 against the cash flow benchmark. In automobile companies, cash flow multiples are half those of reported earnings.
"Our sense is that you've got with the currency tailwind there, liquidity ... building up in their companies enormously," Clough said.
The liquidity rise is especially strong in export-oriented companies "but we think we'll see that in the domestic companies as well."
